county: Los Angeles (footprint straddles the Los Angeles / Orange county line)
disclaimer: Hypothesis-neutral public-records screening. Nothing here asserts that any community is contaminated. The only soil fact anywhere is 'unstudied'. Geographic or temporal overlap does not establish exposure or causation.
earliest_imagery: OLDEST TOPO: USGS 1896 Downey Sheet, California (30-minute quadrangle) is the oldest topographic map that covers the historic Rancho Los Alamitos land. This is not inferred: the Los Cerritos Wetlands EIR Cultural Resources study (LSA/Heck 2017) explicitly reviewed and cited 'the 1896 USGS Downey Sheet, California' in its historic-map review of the former-rancho coastal footprint, and its bibliography lists 'United States Geological Survey (USGS). 1896. Downey Sheet, California.' LAPL's historical-topo research guide corroborates an early Downey-quad series (though it lists the Downey editions it holds as 1902 and later, so the 1896 sheet may be a distinct/earlier printing attested via the EIR and Pastmaps). OLDEST AERIAL: the earliest aerial confirmed to cover this footprint is the 1928 Fairchild Aerial Surveys 'Long Beach Aerial' (cited in the same EIR as 'Fairchild Aerial Surveys. 1928. Long Beach Aerial.' and used to place the Bixby Ranch Field Office at the Seal Beach Oil Field). Regional Fairchild and Spence oblique aerials of the Los Angeles basin exist from 1927 (UCSB Fairchild Aerial Surveys; UCLA Spence collection), and MAY image this parcel, but 1928 is the earliest frame verified against this specific land in this pass. Net: oldest topo = 1896 (USGS Downey Sheet); oldest confirmed aerial = 1928 (Fairchild Long Beach), with possible 1927 regional coverage unverified at frame level.
review_start_year: 1928 (earliest historical aerial reviewed); 1896 (earliest topographic map reviewed) -- per the Los Cerritos Wetlands Oil Consolidation and Restoration Project Draft EIR, Section 3.04 Cultural Resources (City of Long Beach lead agency; SCH #2016041083; cultural study by LSA / Heck 2017; document dated July 2017).
review_gap_note: review_gap_years = 1928 (earliest historical AERIAL photograph the community-scale CEQA review actually examined) minus ~1912 (approximate close of the California cattle-tick arsenical/petroleum dipping and federal-quarantine era). The entire pre-1912 mandated-dipping window sits BELOW the review's aerial floor. The headline document -- the Los Cerritos Wetlands Oil Consolidation and Restoration Project Draft EIR, Sec. 3.04 Cultural Resources (LSA/Heck, July 2017), which covers former Rancho Los Alamitos coastal land straddling the San Gabriel River between Long Beach and Seal Beach -- states verbatim: 'Historic aerial photographs (historicaerials.com) taken in 1928, 1947, 1953, 1963, and 1972 were examined, as was the 1896 USGS Downey Sheet, California, 1925 Long Beach, 1949 and 1964 Los Alamitos topographic maps (USGS 1896, 1925, 1949, 1964, 1981).' So the aerial floor is 1928 and the topo floor is 1896. IMPORTANT QUALIFIERS: (1) This is a cultural-resources / historic-property review, NOT a hazardous-materials Phase I ESA, so a dip facility being below the aerial floor is expected and is a data-availability limitation, not evidence of a hazard. (2) A full-text search of that EIR section for 'dipping', 'arsenic', 'cattle', 'tick', and 'quarantine' returned ZERO hits (the sole 'dip' hit and the many 'vat' substring hits were inside unrelated words such as excavation); the review does not discuss ranch-era stock dipping at all. (3) The gap could be understated: the coastal communities on this land (Seal Beach, Los Alamitos, Rossmoor, Cypress) now sit in ORANGE County, and Orange County was among the very LAST California counties still under federal cattle-tick quarantine (still quarantined as of 1 April 1910), with mandatory arsenical/petroleum dipping under the 1907 California disinfection law, so the effective dip-era floor for this footprint may run to ~1912. (4) Much of the modern residential buildout on this land -- Rossmoor (subdivided 1955-1961 by Ross Cortese), Leisure World Seal Beach (early 1960s), and Los Alamitos -- predates CEQA (enacted 1970; extended to private projects 1972), so no community-wide historical-aerial review of the ranch land was ever performed for the ORIGINAL development; and the current Old Ranch Country Club Specific Plan EIR (City of Seal Beach, NOP dated 26 Jan 2023, on a 155.5-acre remnant of Bixby Ranch Company land) formally scoped Agriculture and Forestry Resources OUT of full analysis.
dipping_records_summary: No record ties a cattle- or sheep-dipping vat to Rancho Los Alamitos or the Bixby ranch operation BY NAME in the public materials searched. Web searches pairing 'Los Alamitos' / 'Bixby' with 'cattle dipping', 'dipping vat', 'arsenical dip', 'sheep scab', and 'tick eradication' returned only (a) generic national/Southern-U.S. (Florida, Texas-Mexico border) dip-vat literature and (b) Los Alamitos / Bixby livestock-and-oil history with no dipping reference. A programmatic full-text query of the California Digital Newspaper Collection ('Los Alamitos' + cattle dipping + tick) could not be completed because the CDNC search endpoint returned HTTP 403 to automated requests during this run (a tooling access limit, NOT a substantive negative). The headline EIR's own historic-record review contains no dipping/vat/arsenic/tick content. What DOES exist is strong COUNTY-LEVEL context but no site-level record: the San Diego History Center's peer-style history of the California cattle-range industry documents that California ran a cattle-tick quarantine and arsenical/petroleum dipping program from 1893 to ~June 1912, that Orange and San Diego counties were the most persistently infested (only San Diego, Orange, Santa Barbara and part of San Luis Obispo remained quarantined by 1 April 1910), and that Los Angeles County was 'the center of meat distribution in the most heavily infected portion of the state.' Conclusion: the searchable materials do not appear to identify a Rancho Los Alamitos dip facility; this is NOT a finding that none existed. The Rancho Los Alamitos Historic Ranch & Gardens (7.5-acre core donated to Long Beach 1967; NRHP 1981) and the Long Beach Public Library / CSULB special collections hold primary Bixby ranch records that were not searched here and are the most likely place any named dipping reference would survive.
sampling_frame_plausibility: Plausibility of an on-ranch stock-handling or dip facility somewhere across the historic footprint is MODERATE-TO-HIGH on terrain and land-use grounds -- but this is a statement about physical plausibility ONLY and asserts NOTHING about whether any vat exists or where. Rancho Los Alamitos was one of the largest livestock operations in California history: under Abel Stearns (from 1844) it was described as the headquarters of the largest cattle ranch in the United States by the early 1850s, and the 1863-64 drought destroyed much of that herd. The Bixby family (John and Jotham Bixby with I.W. Hellman) leased in 1878 and bought in 1881, running sheep (the Bixbys had driven ~2,000 head west in the 1850s), cattle, hogs and horses, and operating Los Alamitos as a cattle FINISHING/fattening ranch, alongside hay, barley, alfalfa, sugar-beet and tenant/truck farming; peak footprint exceeded 28,000 acres spanning today's Long Beach, Los Alamitos, Rossmoor, Seal Beach, Cypress, Stanton and part of Garden Grove. Abundant reliable water existed across the footprint (the San Gabriel River and Coyote Creek, the Los Cerritos and Los Alamitos wetland/lowland systems, and the area's noted artesian/lowland springs -- 'Alamitos' = 'little cottonwoods,' a phreatophyte marking shallow water). Large mixed herds plus reliable water are the physical preconditions for a dip/handling facility, and the specifically-relevant regulatory vector is unusually strong here: the coastal portion of this land is in Orange County, which stayed under federal cattle-tick quarantine with mandated arsenical/petroleum dipping later than almost anywhere else in the state (into 1910-1912). LIMITING CONSIDERATIONS: physical/regulatory plausibility is NOT evidence of existence; no imagery or record reviewed in this pass locates any such facility; a finishing/fattening operation and sheep flocks do not by themselves require an arsenical CATTLE-TICK dip; sheep dips of the era often used lime-sulfur or nicotine rather than arsenic, so even a hypothetical dip's residual chemistry is unknown; and the 1928 aerial floor is already ~16 years after the dipping era closed, so a vat backfilled before 1928 would leave no aerial signature.

findings.claim: HEADLINE: The community-scale CEQA historical land-use review for this footprint (Los Cerritos Wetlands Oil Consolidation and Restoration Project Draft EIR, Sec. 3.04 Cultural Resources, LSA/Heck, July 2017) examined historical aerials only back to 1928 and topographic maps back to 1896, leaving roughly 16 years of the pre-1912 California arsenical/petroleum cattle-tick dipping era entirely below its aerial floor.
findings.supporting: The EIR section states verbatim: 'Historic aerial photographs (historicaerials.com) taken in 1928, 1947, 1953, 1963, and 1972 were examined, as was the 1896 USGS Downey Sheet ... 1925 Long Beach, 1949 and 1964 Los Alamitos topographic maps.' 1928 (earliest aerial) minus ~1912 (close of the dipping/quarantine era) = 16-year unreviewed window. The document covers former Rancho Los Alamitos coastal land straddling the San Gabriel River between Long Beach and Seal Beach.
findings.counter_evidence: This is a cultural-resources / archaeological-and-historic-property review, not a hazardous-materials Phase I ESA; a dip vat sitting below the aerial floor is an expected data-availability limitation, not evidence of a hazard. A full-text search of the section for 'dipping', 'arsenic', 'cattle', 'tick', and 'quarantine' returned zero substantive hits, i.e. the review indicates NO dip facility in any reviewed year (1928 onward) and does not raise the topic. 1928 is also the standard Los Angeles-basin aerial floor (earliest routinely available Fairchild/Spence coverage), so the gap reflects imagery availability, not an omission by the reviewer.
findings.citation: Los Cerritos Wetlands Oil Consolidation and Restoration Project Draft EIR, Sec. 3.04 Cultural Resources (City of Long Beach lead agency; SCH #2016041083), 'Historic Aerial Photograph and Map Review', dated July 2017; longbeach.gov .../los-cerritos-wetlands-restoration-and-oil-consolidation-project/3-04_culturalresources; project record ceqanet.lci.ca.gov/2016041083. Grade A2.

findings.claim: The oldest topographic map covering the historic Rancho Los Alamitos land is the USGS 1896 Downey Sheet, California (30-minute quadrangle).
findings.supporting: The LCW EIR Cultural Resources study explicitly reviewed and cited 'the 1896 USGS Downey Sheet, California' and lists 'USGS. 1896. Downey Sheet, California' in its references; Pastmaps also lists an 1896-era Downey/Los Alamitos sheet as the oldest map for the area.
findings.counter_evidence: At 30-minute / small scale the 1896 sheet is far too coarse to resolve a small dip vat, corral, or working facility; it records regional relief, drainages and named ranchos only, so it neither shows nor rules out any such facility. LAPL's own Downey holdings begin at 1902 (Nov 1902) rather than 1896, so the exact 1896 printing rests on the EIR citation and secondary listings rather than a primary USGS page opened in this run; the coastal/southern rancho land may fall partly on adjacent 1896 sheets (e.g. San Pedro / Las Bolsas) not individually verified here.
findings.citation: LCW EIR Sec. 3.04 Cultural Resources references (USGS 1896 Downey Sheet), July 2017, Grade A2; corroborated by LAPL Historical USGS Topographical Maps of Southern California research guide (B1) and Pastmaps (C). Map itself A1, accessed secondhand.

findings.claim: The earliest aerial confirmed to cover this footprint is the 1928 Fairchild Aerial Surveys 'Long Beach Aerial'; regional Fairchild/Spence aerials exist from 1927 but frame-level coverage of this parcel was not verified.
findings.supporting: The LCW EIR cites 'Fairchild Aerial Surveys. 1928. Long Beach Aerial.' and uses a 1928 Fairchild aerial of the Seal Beach/Synergy Oil Field to locate the Bixby Ranch Field Office. UCSB's Fairchild Aerial Surveys collection and UCLA's Spence collection both hold Los Angeles-basin oblique aerials from 1927.
findings.counter_evidence: 1928 is already ~16 years after the dipping era closed; a vat demolished or backfilled before 1928 would leave no aerial signature, and none is noted in any reviewed frame. Whether the 1927 Fairchild/Spence flights actually image this specific footprint at usable resolution was NOT confirmed frame-by-frame in this pass, so 1927 cannot yet be claimed as coverage of this land. Early Fairchild/Spence frames are largely low-altitude obliques, not systematic vertical mapping coverage.
findings.citation: LCW EIR Sec. 3.04 (Fairchild Aerial Surveys 1928 Long Beach Aerial), July 2017, A2; UCSB Library Fairchild Aerial Surveys (library.ucsb.edu/geospatial) A2; UCLA Spence collection / OAC finding aid A2.

findings.claim: California ran a cattle-tick quarantine and arsenical/petroleum dipping program from 1893 to about June 1912, and the coastal portion of Rancho Los Alamitos now lies in Orange County -- one of the very last counties still under federal quarantine (as of 1 April 1910).
findings.supporting: The San Diego History Center's history of the California cattle-range industry documents: state quarantine law 19 Mar 1893; federal quarantine of the entire state by 22 Jan 1896; treatment by 'chemical dips of petroleum and arsenic'; the 1907 California law mandating disinfection 'according to the directions of the State Veterinary'; that by 1 April 1910 only San Diego, Orange, Santa Barbara and part of San Luis Obispo remained quarantined; that Los Angeles County was 'the center of meat distribution in the most heavily infected portion of the state'; and that the quarantine was substantially lifted by June 1912.
findings.counter_evidence: This is COUNTY/STATE-level history and establishes that the hazard CLASS and era are real and locally applicable; it does NOT place any dip vat on Rancho Los Alamitos land. County-wide quarantine and mandated dipping do not imply a specific on-ranch facility, and the program targeted the cattle-fever tick specifically, whereas Los Alamitos was substantially a finishing/fattening and sheep operation.
findings.citation: San Diego History Center Journal, 'California's Cattle Range Industry: Decimation of the Herds, 1870-1912' (sandiegohistory.org/journal/1965/january/cattle). Grade B1.

findings.claim: Rancho Los Alamitos was among the largest livestock operations in California history -- headquarters of the largest U.S. cattle ranch under Stearns in the 1850s, and a Bixby cattle-finishing and sheep operation from 1878/1881 -- with abundant water across its >28,000-acre footprint, making an on-ranch stock-handling/dip facility physically plausible.
findings.supporting: Multiple histories: Nieto grant 1790, Rancho Los Alamitos formed in the 1834 partition; Abel Stearns acquired it in 1844 and it became headquarters of the largest cattle ranch in the U.S. by the early 1850s (herd largely lost in the 1863-64 drought); the Bixbys (with I.W. Hellman) leased 1878 and bought 1881, running sheep, cattle, hogs and horses and using Los Alamitos as a finishing ranch, plus hay/barley/alfalfa/sugar-beet and tenant farming. Footprint >28,000 acres across Long Beach, Los Alamitos, Rossmoor, Seal Beach, Cypress, Stanton and part of Garden Grove; abundant water (San Gabriel River, Coyote Creek, Los Cerritos/Los Alamitos wetlands, artesian lowlands).
findings.counter_evidence: Physical plausibility is NOT evidence of existence, and no image or record reviewed here locates any dip/corral facility. A finishing/fattening cattle operation and sheep flocks do not necessarily require an arsenical cattle-TICK dip; California's dipping regime, while real and locally mandated, was lighter and shorter than the U.S. South; and sheep dips often used lime-sulfur or nicotine rather than arsenic.
findings.citation: Wikipedia 'Rancho Los Alamitos'; rancholosalamitos.org history; City of Long Beach / LA Conservancy; City of Los Alamitos history page. Grades B2/C.

findings.claim: No dipping vat is tied to Rancho Los Alamitos or the Bixby ranch by name in the public sources searched.
findings.supporting: Targeted web searches pairing 'Los Alamitos'/'Bixby' with dipping/vat/arsenical-dip/sheep-scab/tick returned only generic national and Southern-U.S. dip literature plus Los Alamitos/Bixby livestock-and-oil history with no dipping reference; the headline EIR's historic-record review contains no dip/vat/arsenic/tick content.
findings.counter_evidence: Absence reflects incomplete and partly inaccessible archives, not proof of absence: the CDNC full-text search endpoint returned HTTP 403 to automated queries this run, and the Bixby primary records at Rancho Los Alamitos Historic Ranch & Gardens, the Long Beach Public Library / CSULB special collections, and the California State Veterinarian / County Agricultural Commissioner tick-eradication files were not searched. 'The searchable materials do not appear to identify X' is distinct from 'X did not happen.'
findings.citation: WebSearch queries (see dead_ends); Rancho Los Alamitos Historic Ranch & Gardens (rancholosalamitos.org); Long Beach Public Library / CSULB special collections. Grade C (negative-search inference).

findings.claim: The current CEQA review on remnant Bixby ranch land (Old Ranch Country Club Specific Plan EIR, City of Seal Beach) scoped Agriculture and Forestry Resources OUT of full analysis, and the original mid-century residential buildout on this land (Rossmoor, Leisure World Seal Beach, Los Alamitos) predates CEQA -- so no community-wide historical-aerial review of the ranch land was performed for the original development.
findings.supporting: The Old Ranch Country Club Specific Plan NOP (City of Seal Beach, dated 26 Jan 2023; 155.5-acre site 'Open Space Golf' since the mid-1960s under the Bixby Ranch Company) states the City determined a full-scope EIR was warranted 'except for Agriculture & Forestry.' Rossmoor was subdivided 1955-1961 (Ross Cortese), Leisure World Seal Beach opened in the early 1960s, and Los Alamitos incorporated later -- all before CEQA (1970; extended to private projects 1972).
findings.counter_evidence: Scoping Agriculture/Forestry out of a golf-course redevelopment EIR is routine and appropriate (the site is long-developed open space) and says nothing about historical soil hazards; and a modern project-level Phase I ESA on any of these parcels WOULD review aerials (to the same ~1928 basin floor). Pre-CEQA buildout means no review was required, not that a hazard exists. No historical-review document for the original developments was located because, plausibly, none was ever prepared.
findings.citation: Old Ranch Country Club Specific Plan Project NOP, City of Seal Beach (26 Jan 2023), CEQAnet SCH #285030-style record files.ceqanet.lci.ca.gov/285030-1; Wikipedia 'Rossmoor, California'. Grade A2 (NOP) / B2 (development dates).

findings.claim: The soil status of these communities with respect to any ranch-era dip residue is unstudied; no DTSC/GeoTracker former cattle-dip-vat cleanup listing for this footprint was identified in this pass.
findings.supporting: No Los Alamitos / Long Beach former-ranch cattle-dip-vat cleanup site surfaced in searching. DTSC's own 'Interim Guidance for Sampling Agricultural Properties' documents that historical agricultural arsenic/lead is a recognized residential-redevelopment concern, i.e., the class of hazard is real and screenable.
findings.counter_evidence: DTSC EnviroStor and State Water Board GeoTracker were not exhaustively queried site-by-site for this specific hazard in this run, so absence of a listing is not confirmation of absence; equally, no listing means there is no positive evidence of contamination. The Long Beach/Los Cerritos area DOES carry heavy documented OIL-field environmental legacy (Seal Beach/Synergy oil fields from 1921), which is a separate, well-documented hazard class and not evidence of dip residue. The only defensible soil fact regarding ranch-era dip residue remains 'unstudied'.
findings.citation: DTSC EnviroStor (envirostor.dtsc.ca.gov) and DTSC Agricultural Sampling Guidance; State Water Board GeoTracker (geotracker.waterboards.ca.gov). Grade A2.
